question: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\0 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\4 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. (a) Find $(AB)'$ and $(A'B')$. (b) Prove $(AB)' = B'A'$. (c) Generalize the result for $n\times n$ matrices and explain under what conditions this property holds.
explanation:
First compute $AB$.

$AB = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\4 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.

First row: $2\times1 + (-1)\times4 = -2$, $2\times2 + (-1)\times1 = 3$.

Second row: $0\times1 + 3\times4 = 12$, $0\times2 + 3\times1 = 3$.

Thus $AB = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3\\12 & 3\end{bmatrix}$.

So $(AB)' = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 12\\3 & 3\end{bmatrix}$.

Now compute $A'$ and $B'$.

$A' = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\-1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B' = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\\2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$.

Compute $B'A'$.

$B'A' = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 4\\2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\-1 & 3\end{bmatrix}$.

First row: $1\times2 + 4\times(-1) = -2$, $1\times0 + 4\times3 = 12$.

Second row: $2\times2 + 1\times(-1) = 3$, $2\times0 + 1\times3 = 3$.

Thus $B'A' = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 12\\3 & 3\end{bmatrix}$.

Hence $(AB)' = B'A'$.

(c) For any matrices $A$ and $B$ for which the product $AB$ is defined, $(AB)' = B'A'$. This holds for square or rectangular matrices whenever multiplication is defined.

options.A:
(a) $(AB)'=\begin{bmatrix}-2&12\\3&3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B'A'=\begin{bmatrix}-2&12\\3&3\end{bmatrix}$. Also, $A'B'$ is not the required product for this property.
(b) Hence $(AB)'=B'A'$.
(c) In general, $(AB)'=B'A'$ whenever $AB$ is defined.
options.B:
(a) $(AB)'=\begin{bmatrix}-2&3\\12&3\end{bmatrix}$ and $B'A'=\begin{bmatrix}-2&12\\3&3\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) Hence $(AB)'\ne B'A'$.
(c) The property holds only for diagonal matrices.
options.C:
(a) $(AB)'=A'B'$.
(b) Hence transpose does not reverse order.
(c) The result holds only for $2\times2$ matrices.
options.D:
(a) $(AB)'=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\-1&3\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $(AB)'=A+B$.
(c) The property never holds for rectangular matrices.
